title: Design a URL Shortener
summary: Practise a complete design: create links, redirect safely, then defend collision handling, cache freshness and failure behavior.
body:
## Your practice brief

Design a service that creates short links and redirects visitors to their destination. Before reading the discussion below, spend a timeboxed session explaining requirements, entities, interfaces, a working baseline and two deep dives. Use paper or your own whiteboard; this page does not provide a live interviewer or an AI score.

Agree on these assumptions for this exercise: around 100 million new links per month, redirects much more frequent than creations, seven-character generated aliases, and a 100 ms redirect latency objective in the serving region. Decide how to measure that latency and what traffic percentile the objective covers. Aim for 99.9% redirect availability; explain which dependencies are inside that boundary.

## 1. Requirements and scope

Users can create a link, optionally request a custom alias, and visit an active link. Allow owners to disable a link. Treat analytics as eventually consistent and keep it out of the redirect's critical path. Authentication, abuse reporting and destination validation need policies, but a full analytics dashboard is outside this first design.

Generated aliases should not be sequentially enumerable. A short public URL is not an authorization secret: never use possession of the alias as permission to view private content.

## 2. Entities and interfaces

Store `Link(alias, destination, owner_id, created_at, expires_at, disabled_at)` with a unique index on `alias`. Use `POST /links` to create a mapping and `GET /{alias}` to redirect. Derive ownership from authentication. A repeated creation with the same idempotency key and payload should return the same link; a different payload under that key should conflict. A custom alias already owned by another mapping returns a conflict rather than overwriting it.

## 3. Complete the baseline

A stateless API writes the mapping to a relational database. The unique constraint, not a prior existence check, decides whether an alias is available. The redirect service looks up the alias, checks expiry and disablement, then returns a redirect to the destination. Missing or expired links return an explicit not-found response according to the product policy.

Choose a redirect and cache policy deliberately. A permanently cached redirect can prevent disablement from taking effect promptly. For mutable links, use a temporary redirect with appropriate cache-control rather than assuming every response can be cached forever. Validate allowed destination schemes and consider abuse controls; an open redirect service can be used for phishing.

Start with a database whose write and read capacity you have measured. A distributed counter, a queue and sharding are not mandatory just because the prompt has a large user count.

## 4. Deep dive: alias space and concurrency

Seven Base62 characters provide 62 to the power of 7 possible aliases, roughly 3.5 trillion. That is a namespace size, not a collision-free guarantee. Generate aliases with a cryptographically secure random source, attempt an insert under the unique constraint and retry with a bound on collision. A sequential counter encoded as Base62 is easy to enumerate and does not satisfy the non-sequential requirement by itself.

At 100 million creations per 30-day month, the average is about 39 creates per second; a tenfold peak is about 390. Redirect load is a separate estimate. If the read/write ratio is 100 to 1, average redirects are roughly 3,900 per second. These assumptions inform testing and cache decisions; they are not proof that a particular database can handle the workload.

## 5. Deep dive: hot links and freshness

A cache-aside lookup can remove repeated reads for hot aliases. Bound its size and TTL, handle cache failure without stampeding the database, and avoid using stale cache state forever after a disable operation. An invalidation message can fail, so combine invalidation with a documented TTL or a stronger validation path where the disablement requirement demands it.

If creation writes to a primary but the first redirect reads a lagging replica, the new link may briefly appear missing. Route that lookup to the primary or use another explicit freshness strategy. Adding replicas alone does not solve read-after-write consistency.

## 6. Deep dive: analytics and failure

Record click events asynchronously only if the product accepts the corresponding loss or durability policy. If clicks are billable, a best-effort in-memory event is not enough: durable acceptance changes the latency and availability design. At-least-once delivery can repeat events, so analytics consumers may need event IDs and deduplication.

Monitor redirect latency, errors, cache hit rate, database saturation, collision retries and analytics lag. Explain behavior when the cache is down, the database is unreachable, or a hot alias receives a sudden burst. State which degraded responses are acceptable rather than silently claiming success.

## Review your answer

Can you trace both creation and redirect? Is alias uniqueness atomic? Did you distinguish a public alias from an access token? Does the cache policy support expiry and disablement? Which estimate changed a decision? Name one simpler alternative and one situation that would justify sharding.

This is one defensible design, not the only valid architecture. The reasoning and guarantees matter more than choosing the same products.
keyTakeaways: A unique database constraint handles concurrent alias collisions; Base62 alone does not make sequential IDs unpredictable.
A complete relational baseline can precede caches, replicas and sharding.
Cache and redirect policies must respect link expiry, disablement and read-after-write freshness.
Analytics durability and duplicate handling depend on product requirements.
Use estimates to justify decisions and review the design against its original requirements.
